This is the first of a series of articles on “Discipleship.” Today, Jesus is continuing to call men and women to respond to the simple call, “Follow Me.” Jesus is calling each of us to personally “Follow Me.” In this series, we will explore the depth of this simple command of Jesus. Like the disciples, you will find yourself drawn to follow Jesus.

You may experience both exhilaration and apprehension. Exhilaration, as your journey of faith takes you to heights of love that you have never known. Apprehension, as your faith is tested in new and difficult ways.

There is an emptiness in every human heart that only Jesus can fill. There is a purity and beauty in the life of Jesus that resonates with those heart longings. As we walk with Jesus, we find ourselves being transformed. Old things pass away. All things become new. His life becomes our life. His desires become our desires.

Discipleship is incumbent on the believer. Believing in Jesus, repenting of our sins, and receiving the Lord Jesus into our heart are the first steps into a lifelong journey of faith. Discipleship is not an alternate means of salvation. Following Jesus is the response of a soul set free. Following Jesus is not a carnal attempt to merit eternal life. It is the love response of one who has discovered the source of life.

If you join us on this journey, you will discover that following Jesus will lead us into the valley of decision where we will find ourselves compelled to choose between a life of total surrender to Christ or a life of sin and pleasing self.

And Jesus, walking by the sea of Galilee, saw two brethren, Simon called Peter, and Andrew his brother, casting a net into the sea: for they were fishers. And he saith unto them, Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men. And they straightway left their nets, and followed him. And going on from thence, he saw other two brethren, James the son of Zebedee, and John his brother, in a ship with Zebedee their father, mending their nets; and he called them. And they immediately left the ship and their father, and followed him –Matthew 4:18-22.

Imagine yourself in a ship with one of these brethren. The sun was rising on the eastern horizon. Anticipating another day of fishing the blue waters of the Galilee, you busy yourself with the daily tasks. Fishing has been your life. You are as much at home on the sea as you are in your cottage.

Another day, another catch of fish, and you should be able to keep the creditors at bay for another week. It’s the only life you have ever known. Your father was a fisherman. Your grandfather was a fisherman. It’s a comfortable life. It’s a familiar life.

This morning, as the waves are gently lapping the sandy shoreline, a man approaches. He’s not a total stranger. Everyone knows about Mary’s son. Everyone has an opinion about Mary’s son. He astounds the local rabbi with his knowledge of the scriptures. His character is flawless; He is the friend of all and a stranger to none.

This man, Jesus (that is his name) is drawing near to your ship. As He draws near, He calls out in a rather cheerful voice, “Follow me.”

James looks at John, and together they look to their father Zebedee. His approving nod was all that they needed. Zebedee had worked with his two sons for many years. Perhaps he was hoping that time with the Nazarene would soften the temper of their abrasive characters.

“Follow me, and I will make you fishers of men.” That’s what He called out to Peter and Andrew. They left their little boat full of nets, perhaps tethered to a stump by the shore. What was it about this Man that He could draw disciples after Him with a simple “Follow Me”? Maybe it was a deep longing in the heart of these disciples—a “hope” that following Jesus might fulfill.

Generations of Jewish men had been looking for The Messiah—The Promised One; He who would break the Roman yoke and restore Israel to her former freedom and glory. Jesus was the most promising revolutionary prospect of the day. He would need a following. He would need their help. Little did they realize that day as they dropped their nets and followed Jesus where that journey would lead them. Little did they know that if they followed this Man, they would never be the same.

As Peter, Andrew, James, and John joined with eight others to follow Jesus, they were walking away from the familiar, secure life of the fisherman. They may have thought that following Jesus would be an adventure. They may have thought that after a term of service to the Nazarene, they could return to their fishing boats. As a matter of fact, that is what they did.

After Jesus’ crucifixion and resurrection, He made several appearances to His disciples. They had not yet received the Holy Spirit, and, in the midst of this great uncertainty, they could not resist the allure of the familiar. They decided to go fishing, but much to their consternation they had lost the touch. They fished all night and caught nothing. In the morning Jesus was standing on the shore. He told them to cast on the right side of the ship. They cast and were not able to pull in the nets due to the multitude of fish.

Simon Peter saith unto them, I go a fishing. They say unto him, We also go with thee. They went forth, and entered into a ship immediately; and that night they caught nothing. But when the morning was now come, Jesus stood on the shore: but the disciples knew not that it was Jesus. Then Jesus saith unto them, Children, have ye any meat? They answered him, No. And he said unto them, Cast the net on the right side of the ship, and ye shall find. They cast therefore, and now they were not able to draw it for the multitude of fishes –John 21:3-6.

Have you ever found yourself in a position where you have tried and tried and all your efforts are met with failure? You know what it is to “reach the end of my hoarded resources”. If that is where you find yourself, you are in a position to experience a miracle. God shows himself strong to those who acknowledge their weakness.

When you decide to follow Jesus, He will draw you into such an utter dependence upon Him that you will finally no longer trust in yourself. To become truly like Jesus is to realize with Paul …that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing…. Paul then continues the verse …for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not –Romans 7:18.

Discipleship will lead us into a total abandonment of ourselves to Christ. Just as the disciples could not have fathomed where following Jesus would lead them, neither can we. We make a faith choice. We choose to follow. We commit the details to our Master.

If you want to be like Jesus, you cannot look back. Jesus said: …No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God –Luke 9:62. Peter looked back. He said, “I go a fishing”. Disillusioned following the crucifixion and glorious resurrection, Peter chose to return to the lifestyle that was familiar to him. He went back to fishing and James and John went with him.

When Jesus appeared on the shore after their long night of fruitless toil, He prepared a fish fry for the weary disciples. As Peter sat munching on a charbroiled fish, Jesus turned to him and said, “Peter, do you love Me more than these?” How gently piercing are the words of Jesus.

Peter responded, “Yes Lord, you know that I love you.” Jesus said, “Feed my lambs.” We do not know how much time passed, but Jesus turned to him again, “Peter…” (actually He called him Simon) “Do you love Me?” Peter gave the same staid response. “Yes Lord, you know that I love you”. It was the right answer, but Jesus was interested in more than just a right answer, so He said to him again, “Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou Me?”

Peter finally began to feel that Jesus was asking for something more of him—something that pierced his soul through and through. He had begun following Jesus with the desire to receive from Him. Now Jesus is asking him to reciprocate that love.

Scenes of Caiaphas’ house came before him. He saw Jesus being brutally handled, falsely accused, and spat upon. He heard the angry shouting of the Sanhedrin as they called for Jesus’ death. And then there was that persistent young damsel that challenged him that he was one of Jesus’ disciples. He said to her, “I am not”. Three times he had denied knowing Jesus and now three times Jesus has challenged his love.

In anguish of heart Peter cried out, “Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee”. Jesus said to him, “Feed my sheep”. From that day, Peter was a man with a calling, not only to know Christ for the purpose of receiving from him, but also to emulate him. Discipleship is more than merely knowing about Jesus. Discipleship is walking in his footsteps and identifying with Jesus in his ministry and in his sufferings—truly knowing Him.

Jesus is asking you today, “Do you love me?” We all know the right answer, “Yes, of course, I love Jesus.” Then “Love your neighbor” – “Serve the needy” – “Defer to your brother” – “Forgive the one that has offended you”.

Discipleship is very practical in that it moves us beyond the ideological and causes us to become the very hands and feet of Jesus to those around us.

If in your heart you are thinking, this doesn’t sound very appealing, I would encourage you to focus on the moment and the task at hand. Peter walked with Jesus for three and a half years before he received this call from Jesus. Jesus never calls us without equipping us, and He doesn’t equip us until He determines that we are ready. After the Day of Pentecost, Peter was called, he was prepared, and he was equipped. Then God used him mightily to establish the church.

I would like to call your attention to another attribute of discipleship that is sometimes misplaced. Discipleship is never intended to be drudgery. If you find following Jesus to be hard and toilsome, that is evidence that your love has not yet been perfected.

Jesus’ soul-piercing question to Peter was quite simple, “Do you love Me?” It was as if Jesus was testing Peter. [“I have a job for you, Peter, but a prerequisite for this job is your devoted love for Me.”] Discipleship is a love response to Jesus. Our love for Christ makes service a joy. Toil is pleasant and sacrifice is not a loss.

We can best understand this in the context of human relationships. If you are married and you truly love your husband or your wife, you do not even consider it a sacrifice to work for the mutual benefit of your marriage. In the same way, if we are truly in love with Jesus it is not considered toil to work for him. No sacrifice that we make for the kingdom of heaven is a loss.

I welcome you to join us as we explore the realities of discipleship. We will learn from Christ’s example of forgiveness. We will gain a greater understanding of what it means to walk by faith. Jesus taught us to not worry but to trust. He taught lessons on servant leadership and on cross bearing. There is so much to discover when we are walking with Jesus.

Expect to be changed. The teachings of Jesus are revolutionary in that they run counter to our human impulses. Purpose to allow the life of Christ to become your life and you will be amazed by what God will do for you.

Dette er den første i en serie artikler om «Disippelskap». I dag fortsetter Jesus å kalle menn og kvinner til å svare på den enkle oppfordringen: «Følg meg.» Jesus kaller hver enkelt av oss til personlig å «følge meg.» I denne serien skal vi utforske dybden i dette enkle budet fra Jesus. Som disiplene vil du finne deg selv dratt til å følge Jesus.

Du kan oppleve både begeistring og uro. Begeistring når din trosreise fører deg til kjærlighetens høyder som du aldri har kjent. Uro når din tro blir prøvet på nye og vanskelige måter.

Det er en tomhet i hvert menneskehjerte som bare Jesus kan fylle. Det er en renhet og skjønnhet i Jesu liv som resonnerer med disse hjertelængslene. Etter hvert som vi går med Jesus, opplever vi å bli forvandlet. Det gamle går bort. Alt blir nytt. Hans liv blir vårt liv. Hans ønsker blir våre ønsker.

Disippelskap påligger den troende. Å tro på Jesus, omvende seg fra våre synder og ta imot Herre Jesus i vårt hjerte er de første skrittene inn i en livslang trosreise. Disippelskap er ikke et alternativt middel til frelse. Å følge Jesus er svaret fra en sjel som er satt fri. Å følge Jesus er ikke et kjødelig forsøk på å fortjene evig liv. Det er kjærlighetssvaret fra den som har funnet livets kilde.

Hvis du blir med oss på denne reisen, vil du oppdage at det å følge Jesus vil lede oss inn i beslutningens dal hvor vi blir tvunget til å velge mellom et liv i full overgivelse til Kristus eller et liv i synd og selvbehag.

Og Jesus, mens han gikk ved Genesarets sjø, så han to brødre, Simon som kalles Peter, og Andreas hans bror, som kastet garn i sjøen; for de var fiskere. Og han sier til dem: Følg meg, så vil jeg gjøre dere til menneskefiskere. Og de forlot straks garnene og fulgte ham. Og fra der gikk han videre og så to andre brødre, Jakob, Sebedeus’ sønn, og Johannes hans bror, i et skip sammen med Sebedeus deres far, som reparerte garnene; og han kalte dem. Og de forlot straks skipet og deres far og fulgte ham – Matteus 4:18-22.

Forestill deg at du er i et skip sammen med en av disse brødrene. Solen sto opp i østhimmelen. I forventning om enda en fiskedag på Genesarets blå vann, gjør du deg opptatt med daglige gjøremål. Fiske har vært ditt liv. Du er like hjemme på sjøen som i hytta di.

Enda en dag, enda en fangst av fisk, og du burde kunne holde kreditorene unna en uke til. Det er det eneste livet du noen gang har kjent. Faren din var fisker. Bestefaren din var fisker. Det er et behagelig liv. Det er et kjent liv.

Denne morgenen, mens bølgene mykt slo mot den sandete strandkanten, nærmer en mann seg. Han er ikke en total fremmed. Alle vet om Marias sønn. Alle har en mening om Marias sønn. Han forbløffer byens rabbi med sin kunnskap om Skriften. Hans karakter er feilfri; han er venn av alle og ukjent for ingen.

Denne mannen, Jesus (det er hans navn), nærmer seg skipet ditt. Idet han kommer nær, roper han med en ganske munter stemme: «Følg meg.»

Jakob ser på Johannes, og sammen ser de mot faren Sebedeus. Hans godkjennende nikk var alt de trengte. Sebedeus hadde arbeidet med sine to sønner i mange år. Kanskje håpet han at tid med Nasarenen ville mildne temperementet i deres skarpe væremåte.

«Følg meg, så vil jeg gjøre dere til menneskefiskere.» Det var det han ropte til Peter og Andreas. De forlot sin lille båt full av garn, kanskje fortøyd til en stokk ved strandkanten. Hva var det ved denne mannen som kunne dra disipler etter seg med et enkelt «Følg meg»? Kanskje lå det en dyp lengsel i disiplene—et «håp» om at det å følge Jesus ville gi oppfyllelse.

Generasjoner av jødiske menn hadde ventet på Messias—Den lovede; han som ville bryte den romerske åket og gjenopprette Israel til sin tidligere frihet og herlighet. Jesus var den mest lovende revolusjonære utsikten i samtiden. Han ville trenge en følge. Han ville trenge deres hjelp. Lite visste de den dagen da de kastet garnene og fulgte Jesus hvor den reisen ville føre dem. Lite visste de at hvis de fulgte denne mannen, ville de aldri bli de samme.

Da Peter, Andreas, Jakob og Johannes sluttet seg til åtte andre for å følge Jesus, gikk de bort fra fiskerens velkjente, sikre liv. De kan ha trodd at det å følge Jesus ville bli et eventyr. De kan ha tenkt at etter en tjenestetid hos Nasarenen kunne de vende tilbake til fiskebåtene sine. Og faktisk var det hva de gjorde.

Etter Jesu korsfestelse og oppstandelse viste han seg flere ganger for disiplene. De hadde ennå ikke fått Den Hellige Ånd, og midt i denne store usikkerheten kunne de ikke motstå det kjente. De bestemte seg for å gå ut og fiske, men til sin forbauselse hadde de mistet takten. De fisket hele natten uten å få noe. Om morgenen stod Jesus på stranden. Han ba dem kaste på høyre side av skipet. De kastet og kunne ikke dra garnene opp på grunn av mengden fisk.

Simon Peter sier til dem: Jeg går og fisker. De sier til ham: Vi følger deg også. De gikk da ut og gikk straks i båten; og den natten fikk de ingenting. Men da morgenen var kommet, stod Jesus på stranden; men disiplene kjente ikke at det var Jesus. Da sier Jesus til dem: Barn, har dere noe mat? De svarte ham: Nei. Og han sier til dem: Kast garnet på høyre side av båten, så skal dere finne. De kastet altså, og nå klarte de ikke å dra det opp for fiskemengden – Johannes 21:3-6.

Har du noen gang funnet deg i en situasjon der du har prøvd og prøvd og alle dine anstrengelser ender i fiasko? Du vet hva det er å «nå enden av mine oppsparte krefter». Hvis det er der du befinner deg, er du i en posisjon til å erfare et mirakel. Gud viser seg sterk for dem som erkjenner sin svakhet.

Når du bestemmer deg for å følge Jesus, vil han føre deg inn i en slik fullstendig avhengighet av ham at du endelig ikke lenger stoler på deg selv. Å bli virkelig lik Jesus er å innse med Paulus …at i meg (det vil si i mitt kjød) bor intet godt… Paulus fortsetter så verset …for å ville er hos meg; men å utføre det gode finner jeg ikke – Romerne 7:18.

Disippelskap vil lede oss til en total overgivelse av oss selv til Kristus. Akkurat som disiplene ikke kunne fatte hvor det å følge Jesus ville føre dem, kan heller ikke vi det. Vi tar et trosvalg. Vi velger å følge. Vi overgir detaljene til vår Mester.

Hvis du vil være lik Jesus, kan du ikke se tilbake. Jesus sa: …Ingen som har lagt hånden til plogen og ser tilbake, er skikket for Guds rike – Lukas 9:62. Peter så tilbake. Han sa: «Jeg går og fisker». Desillusjonert etter korsfestelsen og den herlige oppstandelsen, valgte Peter å vende tilbake til den livsstilen som var kjent for ham. Han gikk tilbake til fisket, og Jakob og Johannes gikk med ham.

Da Jesus viste seg på stranden etter deres lange natt med ufruktbart slit, gjorde han opp en fiskemiddag for de trette disiplene. Mens Peter satt og småspiste en grillet fisk, vendte Jesus seg til ham og sa: «Peter, elsker du meg mer enn disse?» Hvor ømt gjennomborende var ikke Jesu ord.

Peter svarte: «Ja Herre, du vet at jeg elsker deg.» Jesus sa: «Gjør mine lam til del.» Vi vet ikke hvor mye tid som gikk, men Jesus vendte seg igjen til ham: «Peter…» (egentlig kalte han ham Simon) «elsker du meg?» Peter ga det samme faste svaret: «Ja Herre, du vet at jeg elsker deg.» Det var riktig svar, men Jesus ville ha mer enn bare et riktig svar, så han sa igjen til ham: «Simon, Jonas’ sønn, elsker du meg?»

Peter begynte endelig å føle at Jesus krevde noe mer av ham—noe som gjennomboret hans sjel på dypet. Han hadde begynt å følge Jesus med et ønske om å motta fra ham. Nå ba Jesus ham om å svare denne kjærligheten.

Scener fra Kajafas hus kom for hans indre syn. Han så Jesus bli mishandlet brutalt, falskt anklaget og spyttet på. Han hørte den rasende ropingen fra sannhetsrådet mens de krevde Jesu død. Og så var det den vedvarende unge piken som utfordret ham og sa at han var en av Jesu disipler. Han sa til henne: «Det er jeg ikke». Tre ganger hadde han fornektet å kjenne Jesus, og nå tre ganger utfordrer Jesus hans kjærlighet.

I hjerteskjærende kval ropte Peter: «Herre, du vet alt; du vet at jeg elsker deg.» Jesus sier til ham: «Gjør mine sauer til del.» Fra den dag var Peter en mann med en kall—ikke bare å kjenne Kristus for å motta fra ham, men også å etterligne ham. Disippelskap er mer enn å vite om Jesus. Disippelskap er å gå i hans fotspor og identifisere seg med Jesus i hans tjeneste og i hans lidelser—virkelig å kjenne ham.

Jesus spør deg i dag: «Elsker du meg?» Vi kjenner alle det riktige svaret: «Ja, selvfølgelig, jeg elsker Jesus.» Så «elsk din neste» – «tjener de trengende» – «ettergi din bror» – «tilgi den som har fornærmet deg».

Disippelskap er svært praktisk ved at det fører oss utover det ideologiske og gjør oss til Jesu hender og føtter for dem rundt oss.

Hvis du i ditt hjerte tenker, dette høres ikke særlig tiltalende ut, vil jeg oppmuntre deg til å fokusere på øyeblikket og oppgaven foran deg. Peter vandret med Jesus i tre og et halvt år før han mottok dette kall fra Jesus. Jesus kaller oss aldri uten å utruste oss, og han utruster oss ikke før han fastslår at vi er klare. Etter pinsedagen ble Peter kalt, forberedt og utrustet. Så brukte Gud ham mektig til å grunnlegge kirken.

Jeg vil gjerne rette din oppmerksomhet mot en annen egenskap ved disippelskap som noen ganger blir misforstått. Disippelskap er aldri ment å være trått arbeid. Hvis du finner det vanskelig og slitsomt å følge Jesus, er det bevis på at din kjærlighet ennå ikke er fullkomnet.

Jesu sjelsgjennomtrengende spørsmål til Peter var ganske enkelt: «Elsker du meg?» Det var som om Jesus testet Peter. [«Jeg har en oppgave til deg, Peter, men et krav for denne oppgaven er din hengivne kjærlighet til meg.»] Disippelskap er et kjærlighetssvar til Jesus. Vår kjærlighet til Kristus gjør tjenesten til glede. Arbeid er behagelig og offer er ikke et tap.

Vi forstår dette best i menneskelige relasjoner. Er du gift og virkelig elsker din mann eller din kone, betraktes det ikke engang som et offer å arbeide for ekteskapets gjensidige beste. På samme måte, hvis vi virkelig er forelsket i Jesus, anses det ikke som anstrengelse å tjene ham. Intet offer vi gir for himmelrikets rike er et tap.

Jeg ønsker deg velkommen til å bli med oss mens vi utforsker realitetene i disippelskap. Vi vil lære av Kristi eksempel på tilgivelse. Vi vil få en større forståelse av hva det betyr å gå ved tro. Jesus lærte oss å ikke bekymre oss, men å stole. Han underviste i tjenerlederskap og i å bære kors. Det er så mye å oppdage når vi går med Jesus.

Forvent å bli forandret. Jesu lære er revolusjonerende ved at den går imot våre menneskelige impulser. Bestem deg for å la Kristi liv bli ditt liv, og du vil bli forundret over hva Gud vil gjøre for deg.

Or can you see the distances so great
Which stretch the mind almost to breaking point
And make you feel the size you really are?
In the still silence of the spacious sky,
The far-off planets seem almost in reach
Compared to the great distance to the stars.
The crescent moon is closer yet to you,
And yet it took man three whole days to reach
That tiny sphere so very close at hand.
But what you see while gazing up to heights
Which you cannot begin to comprehend
Is but a streak of all the vast expanse
Beyond the knowledge of this human race.
And so, my friend, I hope that you will feel
That greatness, vastness, emptiness of space
Which our Creator made for us so we
Can feel His greatness and His tender love
And humbly bow our heads and worship Him.

–by Daniel Kaufman

Когда ты, мой друг, стоишь на этой земле
И смотришь в небосвод в вышине,
Где простирается весь простор, что видишь ты?
Большое чёрное одеяло, натянутое над небом,
С множеством загадочных огоньков где‑то там?
Или видишь ты гигантские расстояния,
Что ум почти доводят до предела и ломают,
И заставляют ощущать, какой ты на самом деле мал?
В тишине безбрежного, просторного неба
Далёкие планеты кажутся почти в досягаемости
По сравнению с огромной далью звёзд.
Серп луны ближе ещё к тебе,
И всё же человеку потребовалось три целых дня,
Чтобы достигнуть той крошечной сферы, так близко лежащей.
Но то, что ты видишь, глядя вверх на ту высоту,
Которую ты не в силах даже начать понять,
— лишь полоска от всего этого безбрежья
За пределами познания этого человеческого рода.
И потому, мой друг, я надеюсь, что ты ощутишь
Величие то, необъятность, пустоту пространства,
Которые наш Творец создал для нас, чтобы мы
Могли почувствовать Его величие и Его нежную любовь
И смиренно склонить головы наши и поклониться Ему.

— Дэниел Кауфман

It’s been said that in the 1500s, after baptism, the Anabaptists lived an average of only 27 days. They were hunted and killed. They realized one thing—serving Christ would most certainly cost them everything. They forsook the comforts of easy living; they forsook it all. It could also have been a similar situation when Jesus walked on the earth, or shortly after He was killed.

…and he turned, and said unto them, If any man come to me, and hate not his father, and mother, and wife, and children, and brethren, and sisters, yea, and his own life also, he cannot be my disciple. And whosoever doth not bear his cross, and come after me, cannot be my disciple. For which of you, intending to build a tower, sitteth not down first, and counteth the cost, whether he have sufficient to finish it? Lest haply, after he hath laid the foundation, and is not able to finish it, all that behold it begin to mock him, Saying, This man began to build, and was not able to finish. Or what king, going to make war against another king, sitteth not down first, and consulteth whether he be able with ten thousand to meet him that cometh against him with twenty thousand? Or else, while the other is yet a great way off, he sendeth an ambassage, and desireth conditions of peace. So likewise, whosoever he be of you that forsaketh not all that he hath, he cannot be my disciple –Luke 14:25-33.

Jesus clearly asked His disciples to count the cost. And they must have counted the cost, for they faithfully gave all, including their lives, for Christ’s Kingdom. They realized they could have had the good things in this life; however, they also realized it would cost them the good things in the next.

Yea, and all that will live godly in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution –2 Timothy 3:12. If we look at the promises which Jesus gave us in His Word about persecution, and then compare them with the lives of Jesus’ followers today, we might be confused. And rightfully so.

He that saith he abideth in him ought himself also so to walk, even as he walked –1 John 2:6. Jesus says we should walk as He walked, He also tells us that we need to follow Him.

How did He walk? We know that Jesus had no place to lay His head—this was how He wanted it. We know that Jesus could have chosen to live where and how He wanted. He was, in fact, in control of the whole world, yet He was despised and rejected by the world and its system. When He spoke, people wanted to lay their hands on Him; they wanted to kill Him. He was not a popular person; He had few friends. In reality, He didn’t fit in, and He didn’t last long. Three years after His ministry began, He was killed. …He was numbered with the transgressors –Mark 15:28.

What about His followers today? Are they walking how He walked? And if not, why not?

We read about the children of Israel going through the wilderness. They fought and overtook the cities in their paths, killing all in the process. We read many accounts about how God instructed the children of Israel to kill all of the enemy, even the women and children. The following is one such account of many.

So the LORD our God delivered into our hands Og also, the king of Bashan, and all his people: and we smote him until none was left to him remaining. And we took all his cities at that time, there was not a city which we took not from them, threescore cities, all the region of Argob, the kingdom of Og in Bashan. All these cities were fenced with high walls, gates, and bars; beside unwalled towns a great many. And we utterly destroyed them, as we did unto Sihon king of Heshbon, utterly destroying the men, women, and children, of every city –Deuteronomy 3:3-6.

We read accounts like this in scripture, and it can cause us to cringe. It is almost as if life itself was not important. Even in the New Testament, death doesn’t seem to be that big of a deal. People lived and people died.

The first week after we moved to Haiti, I was driving through the city. Suddenly, right in front of me I saw a man lying in the street. Blood ran down the road and pooled in a low spot—he was dead. I was shocked. But what shocked me the most was that no one seemed to notice. People by the hundreds busily walked around him, not even looking at the man—no one cared.

Over the next six years we saw many dead or dying people—it became a normal scene.

If that was how it was back in the Bible times, and it is still how it is today in many countries of the world, maybe we are the ones that are out of the norm? Maybe we esteem life higher than God does. Maybe we are among those that Jesus spoke of when He said—He that loveth his life shall lose it; and he that hateth his life in this world shall keep it unto life eternal –John 12:25.

In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread, till thou return unto the ground; for out of it wast thou taken: for dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return –Genesis 3:19. We were created out of the dust, and after a few short years, we return to the very same dust.

Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away –James 4:14. The Bible also calls our lives a vapor.

We all know what happens after that—the judgment, then eternity. So why do we care so much about this life? Maybe it is an American problem or a western problem.

It is obvious that Americans are looked upon as ‘more valuable’ than most other nationalities. If you are an American in a developing country, you are heralded as a king. If something happens to an American, it is quickly headline news. I once stood over the bodies of two murdered men. One of their close friends stood by, so I asked him how he was doing. He shrugged and said, “This is life”.

So why does life mean so much to us Americans? The answer is simple. We can obtain almost anything we want; money is easy to get, and we can live how we want. We can live in pleasure every day. We go to the store and buy what we want, when we want—we have it our way. This is just how it is; for most of us it is all we have ever known—the life of plenty. So how does this affect us?

This type of living makes it especially hard to ‘give all’ for Christ. It makes it difficult to obey Jesus’ command to …Go ye into all the world, and preach the gospel to every creature –Mark 16:15. It makes it difficult to say with the Apostle Paul, For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain –Philippians 1:21. In reality, it makes it difficult to be a Christian.

When Jesus said… For whosoever will save his life shall lose it: and whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it –Matthew 16:25, what did He mean? Could it mean literally just what it says: that when you fall in love with your own life, you cannot effectively follow Christ, so that in the end you will actually lose your life?

Can you go to the lost and forsake the comforts of this life if it’s those comforts that you love and live for? It’s not likely. What we have is “Americanized” Christians that will only go to the mission field if they can take their comforts with them. This produces rich, comfortable missionaries who, despite their best efforts, can’t win the lost, rather they make them jealous. Can we go into the cities and preach the gospel to the lost like so many before us have? Can we take time to teach and disciple the tens of thousands who are seeking? If we love our lives, we probably will not, since there is too much to lose and it’s a waste of good talent and opportunity. God help us.

When we are living to please the flesh and we have our lives figured out, it is hard for God to use us. We are puffed up. We tend to believe that God has blessed us because of all our possessions and our status in life; but isn’t this the prosperity gospel? What if that changed? Would we still consider ourselves to be blessed? Is it God or our own doing that causes us to be joyful? What if we found ourselves in John the Baptist’s shoes? Or the Apostle Paul’s? If we would be sitting in prison for doing nothing wrong, would our joy remain? It should if the Holy Spirit is living and working in our hearts. The Bible says that we can suffer joyfully!

Years ago, a coworker of mine was a happy fellow. He had a nice life. There was one problem—he did not believe there was a God. We would talk day after day. He would constantly tell me how happy he was and that one didn’t need to be a Christian to be happy. He would talk about his nice life, all that he possessed, his good job, his nice family. Interestingly enough, he truly did seem happy.

I would tell him that true happiness didn’t come from the things that we possess or the position that we find ourselves in, but he would just disagree. He also proclaimed that he lived a better life than most Christians that he knew. He also said he didn’t get angry like most Christians and could control himself. I tried to convince him that he was deceived. At times I would think I was getting somewhere with him, then later it would seem I was far from reaching him. One day he soberly admitted that I seemed to be different that most Christians he had known in the past, but that still wasn’t enough.

I left that job and lost contact with him. Recently, I ran into another one of my former coworkers. I quickly thought of my friend and asked how he was doing. He looked at me strangely and then shocked me to my core as he said, “He committed suicide”.

The devil wants us to love our life—it’s that simple. When we love our life, we focus on it, we cherish it. The last thing we want to do is lose our life, even if it is for something eternal.

When I was in the Marines, they would constantly remind us that our lives were not number one; our country was. There are many young men who put their country first. Many have gone and given their all; many have died.

In World War 2, the Japanese would try to sneak up to a fox hole housing soldiers and throw in a grenade. Many times, it didn’t end like the Japanese wanted, because someone would jump on the grenade, absorbing the explosion. Thousands gave their lives to save their friends and defend their country. But be sure, if their priorities were not in order (of country first before themselves), they would not have done so.

If someone today, in America, would risk their life for the sake of the gospel, he would be labeled as foolish, reckless, and immature. But what do we say about so many before us—the ones that gave their lives while standing for the same things that we say we believe today? And what about the thousands today who are putting their lives on the line in other countries—are they foolish? Let’s look at a very obvious example in Acts.

And as we tarried there many days, there came down from Judaea a certain prophet, named Agabus. And when he was come unto us, he took Paul’s girdle, and bound his own hands and feet, and said, Thus saith the Holy Ghost, So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle, and shall deliver him into the hands of the Gentiles. And when we heard these things, both we, and they of that place, besought him not to go up to Jerusalem. Then Paul answered, What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem for the name of the Lord Jesus. –Acts 21:10-13.

What would we think of Paul’s actions today? Paul went to Jerusalem and was quickly taken, beaten, and put in prison. It was the beginning of the end for our dear brother. He was moved from prison to prison and eventually ended up in Rome where he was beheaded. What do you think the ones that tried to persuade him to not go to Jerusalem thought? Do you think they called him a fool? Did they shake their heads and say, “I told him not to go!”?

We cannot know for sure. However, I am sure that Paul was simply putting the kingdom of Christ first; his life did not matter. He was obeying God, and God had told him to go.

When we love our lives, it is very difficult to be an effective disciple of the Lord Jesus. We end up forsaking God’s calling and then we are stuck trying to live the Christian life alone, and without God—no spiritual help from above, causing us to fall way short of the mark.

It’s ironic that only when we forsake all, including our lives, will we find true peace and purpose for our lives. And when we love our lives, that is when we will lose them.

Rise up, O saints of God!
Have done with lesser things.
Give heart and soul and mind and strength
To serve the King of kings.

Rise up, O saints of God!
The kingdom tarries long.
Bring in the day of Christlike love
And end the night of wrong.

Lift high the cross of Christ!
Tread where His feet have trod.
Led onward by the Son of Man,
Rise up, O saints of God!

Let us rise up, as God’s people, and begin to be done with lesser things, with our gaze on things above, not on the things of this earth. Yes, we will stand out; we will be labeled fools and many other things. However, we will once again catch God’s attention and the fires of revival will once again burn!

Daar word gesê dat in die 1500's, ná die doop, die Anabaptiste gemiddeld net 27 dae geleef het. Hulle is gejaag en vermoor. Hulle het een ding besef—die bediening van Christus sou hulle sekerlik alles kos. Hulle het die gerief van maklike lewe verlaat; hulle het dit alles verlaat. Dit kon ook ’n soortgelyke situasie gewees het toe Jesus op die aarde gewandel het, of kort nadat Hy gedood is.

…en Hy het omgedraai en vir hulle gesê: As iemand tot My wil kom en haat nie sy vader en moeder en vrou en kinders en broers en susters, ja, ook sy eie lewe nie, kan hy nie my leerling wees nie. En wie nie sy kruis dra en My nakom nie, kan nie my leerling wees nie. Want wie van julle wil ’n toring bou, sit nie eers neer en bereken die koste, of hy genoeg het om dit te voltooi nie? Anders, nadat hy die fondament gelê het en nie kan voltooi nie, begin almal wat dit sien, hom bespot en sê: Hierdie man het begin bou en kon dit nie voltooi nie. Of watter koning, wat teen ’n ander koning oorlog gaan maak, sit nie eers neer en beraadslaag of hy met tienduisend diegene kan ontmoet wat met twintigduisend teen hom kom nie? Of anders terwyl die ander nog ver is, stuur hy ’n ambassadeur en versoek vredevoorwaardes. Net so kan geen een van julle wat nie al sy besittings verlaat nie, my leerling wees nie – Lukas 14:25-33.

Jesus het duidelik Sy dissipels gevra om die koste te bereken. En hulle moes die koste bereken het, want hulle het getrou alles gegee, insluitend hulle lewens, vir Christus se Koninkryk. Hulle het besef hulle kon die goeie dinge in hierdie lewe hê; tog het hulle ook besef dit sou hulle die goeie dinge in die volgende lewe kos.

En ook almal wat godsalig in Christus Jesus wil leef, sal vervolging ly –2 Timoteus 3:12. As ons na die beloftes kyk wat Jesus ons in Sy Woord oor vervolging gegee het, en dit vergelyk met die lewens van Jesus se volgelinge vandag, kan ons verward raak. En regmatig so.

Wie bewering maak dat hy in Hom bly, behoort self ook so te wandel soos Hy gewandel het –1 Johannes 2:6. Jesus sê ons moet wandel soos Hy gewandel het; Hy sê ons moet Hom volg.

Hoe het Hy gewandel? Ons weet dat Jesus geen plek gehad het om Sy hoof op te lê nie—dit was hoe Hy dit wou hê. Ons weet dat Jesus kon gekies het om te woon waar en hoe Hy wou. Hy het inderdaad beheer oor die hele wêreld gehad, tog is Hy verag en verwerp deur die wêreld en sy stelsel. Toe Hy gepreek het, wou mense hulle hande op Hom lê; hulle wou Hom doodmaak. Hy was nie ’n populêre persoon nie; Hy het min vriende gehad. In werklikheid het Hy nie ingepas nie, en Hy het nie lank gebly nie. Drie jaar nadat Sy bediening begin het, is Hy gedood. …Hy is saam met die oortreders getel – Markus 15:28.

Wat van Sy volgelinge vandag? Wandel hulle soos Hy gewandel het? En indien nie, waarom nie?

Ons lees van die kinders van Israel wat deur die wildernis trek. Hulle het geveg en die stede op hulle pad oorwin en almal in die proses gedood. Ons lees baie berigte hoe God die kinders van Israel beveel het om al die vyand te vernietig, ook die vroue en kinders. Die volgende is een so ’n rekening van baie.

So het die HERE, ons God, ook Og, die koning van Bashan, en al sy volk in ons hande oorgelewer: en ons het hom geslaan, totdat geen oorblywendes aan hom oor was nie. En ons het al sy stede destyds verower; daar was geen stad wat ons nie van hulle verower het nie, sestig stede, die hele streek van Argob, die koningskap van Og in Bashan. Al hierdie stede was omhein met hoë mure, hekke en sluitings; behalwe onomheinde dorpe, baie van hulle. En ons het hulle volkome uitgeroei, soos ons ook aan Sihon, die koning van Heshbon, gedoen het, deur die mans, vroue en kinders van elke stad volkome te vernietig – Deuteronomium 3:3-6.

Ons lees sulke rekords in die Skrif, en dit kan ons laat wegkruip. Dit is amper asof die lewe self nie belangrik was nie. Selfs in die Nuwe Testament lyk dit asof die dood nie so ’n groot saak was nie. Mense het geleef en mense het gesterf.

Die eerste week nadat ons na Haïti verhuis het, het ek deur die stad gery. Skielik, net voor my siening, het ek ’n man in die straat sien lê. Bloed het die pad af geloop en in ’n laer plek opgehoop—hy was dood. Ek was geskok. Maar wat my die meeste geskok het, was dat niemand dit hardlykse opgemerk het nie. Mense het honderde te wyte uitgeroer en besig verby hom geloop, sonder om eers na die man te kyk—niemand het omgegee nie.

Oor die volgende ses jaar het ons baie dooies of sterwendes gesien—dit het ’n normale tafereel geword.

As dit hoe dit in Bybelse tye was, en dit steeds so is vandag in baie lande van die wêreld, dalk is ons die wat buite die norm is? Miskien ag ons die lewe hoër as wat God dit ag. Miskien is ons onder diegene waarvan Jesus gepraat het toe Hy gesê het—Hy wat sy lewe liefhet, sal dit verloor; en hy wat sy lewe haat in hierdie wêreld, sal dit bewaar tot die ewigheid – Johannes 12:25.

Met die sweet van jou aangesig sal jy jou brood eet, totdat jy tot die grond terugkeer; want uit dit is jy geneem: want stof is jy, en tot stof sal jy terugkeer – Genesis 3:19. Ons is uit die stof geskape, en na ’n paar kort jare keer ons terug na daardie stof.

En julle weet nie wat môre sal wees. Wat is julle lewe? Dit is tog ’n damp wat skyn vir ’n tydjie en dan verdwyn – Jakobus 4:14. Die Bybel noem ons lewe ook ’n damp.

Ons weet almal wat daarna gebeur—die oordeel, en dan die ewigheid. Waarom gee ons dan so baie om oor hierdie lewe? Miskien is dit ’n Amerikaanse probleem of ’n westerse probleem.

Dit is duidelik dat Amerikaners as ’meer waardevol’ beskou word as meeste ander nasionaliteite. As jy ’n Amerikaan in ’n ontwikkelende land is, word jy soos ’n koning verhef. As iets met ’n Amerikaan gebeur, maak dit gou kopkrante nuus. Ek het eens bo die liggame van twee vermoorde mans gestaan. Een van hulle naby vriende het daar bygestaan, so ek het hom gevra hoe dit met hom gaan. Hy het sy skouers opgehaag en gesê, “Dit is die lewe”.

Waarom beteken lewe dus so baie vir ons Amerikaners? Die antwoord is eenvoudig. Ons kan byna enigiets verkry wat ons wil hê; geld is maklik om te kry, en ons kan lewe soos ons wil. Ons kan elke dag in plesier leef. Ons gaan na die winkel en koop wat ons wil, wanneer ons wil—ons kry dit op ons manier. Dit is net hoe dit is; vir die meeste van ons is dit alles wat ons nog ooit geken het—the lewe van oorvloed. Hoe beïnvloed dit ons?

Hierdie tipe lewe maak dit besonder moeilik om “alles te gee” vir Christus. Dit maak dit moeilik om Jesus se opdrag te gehoorsaam—Gaan julle in die hele wêreld en verkondig die evangelie aan alle mense – Markus 16:15. Dit maak dit moeilik om saam met die apostel Paulus te sê, Want my lewe is Christus en my sterwe is wins – Filippense 1:21. In werklikheid maak dit dit moeilik om ’n Christen te wees.

Toe Jesus gesê het… Want een wie sy lewe wil bewaar, sal dit verlore maak; en wie sy lewe verloor ter wille van My, sal dit vind – Matteus 16:25, wat het Hy bedoel? Kon dit letterlik beteken wat dit sê: dat as jy jou eie lewe liefkry, jy Christus nie effektief kan volg nie, sodat jy uiteindelik jou lewe sal verloor?

Kan jy na die verlore gaan en die gerief van hierdie lewe verlaat as dit daardie gerief is waarna jy streef en vir wie jy leef? Dit is onwaarskynlik. Wat ons het, is “ge-Amerikaniseerde” Christene wat slegs na die sendingveld sal gaan as hulle hul geriewe saam kan neem. Dit produseer ryk, gerieflike sendelinge wat, ondanks hulle beste pogings, die verlore nie kan wen nie; inteendeel, hulle maak hulle jaloers. Kan ons na die stede gaan en die evangelie aan die verlore verkondig soos soveel voor ons gedoen het? Kan ons tyd neem om die tienduisende te leer en te dissiplineer wat soek? As ons ons lewens liefhet, sal ons dit waarskynlik nie doen nie, want daar is te veel om te verloor en dit is ’n vermorsing van goeie talente en geleenthede. God help ons.

Wanneer ons leef om die vlees te behaag en ons het ons lewens uitgewerk, is dit moeilik vir God om ons te gebruik. Ons is opgeblase. Ons neig om te glo dat God ons geseën het as gevolg van al ons besittings en ons status; maar is dit nie die welvaartsleer nie? Wat as dit verander het? Sou ons ons nog steeds as geseënd beskou? Is dit God of ons eie doen wat ons vreugde veroorsaak? Wat as ons onsself in Johannes die Doper se skoene bevind? Of die apostel Paulus se? As ons in die tronk sit omdat ons niks verkeerds gedoen het nie, sou ons vreugde bly? Dit behoort so te wees as die Heilige Gees in ons harte woon en werk. Die Bybel sê ons kan vreugdevol ly!

Jare gelede was ’n medewerker van my ’n gelukkige man. Hy het ’n aangename lewe gehad. Daar was een probleem—hy het nie geglo daar is ’n God nie. Ons het dag na dag gesels. Hy het voortdurend vir my gesê hoe gelukkig hy was en dat ’n mens nie ’n Christen hoef te wees om gelukkig te wees nie. Hy het gepraat oor sy goeie lewe, alles wat hy besit het, sy goeie werk, sy aangename familie. Interessant genoeg het hy regtig lyk of hy gelukkig was.

Ek het vir hom gesê dat ware geluk nie van die goed kom wat ons besit nie of die posisie waarin ons ons bevind nie, maar hy het net verskil van mening. Hy het ook beweer dat hy ’n beter lewe as die meeste Christene wat hy geken het, gelei het. Hy het ook gesê hy raak nie so kwaad soos die meeste Christene en kon homself beheer nie. Ek het probeer hom oortuig dat hy mislei was. Soms sou ek dink ek maak vordering met hom, en later sou dit lyk of ek ver van hom af was. Een dag het hy ernstig erken dat ek skynbaar anders was as die meeste Christene wat hy in die verlede geken het, maar dit was steeds nie genoeg nie.

Ek het daardie werk verlaat en kontak met hom verloor. Onlangs het ek ’n ander voormalige kollega raakgeloop. Ek het vinnig aan my vriend gedink en gevra hoe dit met hom gaan. Hy het my vreemd aangekyk en my tot in die kern geskok toe hy gesê het, “Hy het selfmoord gepleeg”.

Die duiwel wil hê ons moet ons lewe liefhet—so eenvoudig is dit. Wanneer ons ons lewe liefhet, fokus ons daarop, ons koester dit. Die laaste ding wat ons wil doen, is om ons lewe te verloor, selfs al is dit vir iets ewigs.

Toe ek by die Mariniers was, het hulle ons voortdurend herinner dat ons lewens nie nommer een was nie; ons land was. Daar is baie jong mans wat hul land eerste stel. Baie het gegaan en alles gegee; baie het gesterf.

Tydens die Tweede Wêreldoorlog het die Japannese probeer om stil-stil by ’n loopgraaf met soldate nader te sluip en ’n granaat in te gooi. Baie kere het dit nie gegaan soos die Japannese wou nie, want iemand het op die granaat gespring en die ontploffing geabsorbeer. Duisende het hulle lewens gegee om hulle vriende te red en hul land te verdedig. Maar wees seker, as hulle prioriteite nie in orde was nie (land eerste, voor hulself), sou hulle dit nie gedoen het nie.

As iemand vandag, in Amerika, sy lewe vir die evangelie sou waag, sou hy as dwaas, roekeloos en onvolwassen gestempel word. Maar wat sê ons oor soveel voor ons—diegene wat hulle lewens gegee het terwyl hulle staan vir dieselfde dinge wat ons vandag sê ons glo? En wat van die duisende vandag wat hul lewens op die spel sit in ander lande—is hulle dwaas? Kom ons kyk na ’n baie duidelike voorbeeld in Handelinge.

En terwyl ons daar baie dae vertoef het, het ’n sekere profeet van Judea, met die naam Agabus, na ons afgekom. En toe hy by ons kom, het hy Paulus se gordel geneem en sy eie hande en voete gebind en gesê: So spreek die Heilige Gees dat die Jode in Jerusalem die man wat hierdie gordel het, sal bind en hom in die hande van die heidene sal uitlewer. En toe ons dit gehoord het, het ons en die inwoners van daardie plek hom be smeek om nie na Jerusalem op te gaan nie. Toe het Paulus geantwoord: Waarom huil julle en breek julle my hart? Want ek is gereed nie net om gebind te word nie, maar ook om in Jerusalem te sterf ter wille van die Naam van die Here Jesus. – Handelinge 21:10-13.

Wat sou ons van Paulus se optrede vandag dink? Paulus het na Jerusalem gegaan en is gou gevange geneem, geslaan en in die tronk gesit. Dit was die begin van die einde vir ons liewe broer. Hy is van tronk na tronk oorgeplaas en het uiteindelik in Rome geëindig waar hy onthoof is. Wat dink jy het diegene wat probeer het om hom te oortuig om nie na Jerusalem te gaan nie, gedink? Dink jy hulle het hom ’n dwaas genoem? Het hulle hulle kop geskud en gesê: “Ek het hom gesê om nie te gaan nie!”?

Ons kan nie seker weet nie. Maar ek is seker dat Paulus eenvoudig Christus se koninkryk eerste gestel het; sy lewe het nie saak gemaak nie. Hy het God gehoorsaam, en God het hom gesê om te gaan.

Wanneer ons ons lewens liefhet, is dit baie moeilik om ’n effektiewe leerling van die Here Jesus te wees. Ons eindig deur God se roeping te verlaat en dan sit ons vas om die christelike lewe alleen te leef, en sonder God—geen geestelike hulp van bo nie, wat veroorsaak dat ons ver onder die merk faal.

Dit is ironies dat net wanneer ons alles, insluitend ons lewens, prysgee, ons ware vrede en doel in ons lewens sal vind. En wanneer ons ons lewens liefhet, is dit wanneer ons dit sal verloor.

Staan op, o heiliges van God!
Wees klaar met mindere dinge.
Gee hart en siel en verstand en krag
Om die Koning van konings te dien.

Staan op, o heiliges van God!
Die koninkryk vertraag lank.
Bring die dag van Christus-agtige liefde in
En beëindig die nag van onreg.

Lig hoog die kruis van Christus!
Loop daar waar Sy voete getree het.
Gelei vorentoe deur die Seun van die Mens,
Staan op, o heiliges van God!

Kom ons staan op, as God se volk, en begin klaar wees met mindere dinge, met ons oog op die dinge daarbo, nie op die dinge van hierdie aarde nie. Ja, ons sal uitstaan; ons sal as dwaas en baie ander dinge bestempel word. Tog sal ons weer God se aandag trek en die vlamme van herlewing sal weer brand!

When you, my friend, are standing on this earth
And gazing up into the firmament
Where stretches all of space, what do you see?
A great black blanket stretched o’er all the sky
With many a mystery light somewhere up there?
Or can you see the distances so great
Which stretch the mind almost to breaking point
And make you feel the size you really are?
In the still silence of the spacious sky,
The far-off planets seem almost in reach
Compared to the great distance to the stars.
The crescent moon is closer yet to you,
And yet it took man three whole days to reach
That tiny sphere so very close at hand.
But what you see while gazing up to heights
Which you cannot begin to comprehend
Is but a streak of all the vast expanse
Beyond the knowledge of this human race.
And so, my friend, I hope that you will feel
That greatness, vastness, emptiness of space
Which our Creator made for us so we
Can feel His greatness and His tender love
And humbly bow our heads and worship Him.

–by Daniel Kaufman

Wanneer jij, mijn vriend, op deze aarde staat
En omhoog tuurt in het firmament

Ver buiten het weten van dit mensenras.

Die grootsheid, uitgestrektheid, leegte van de ruimte
Die onze Schepper voor ons maakte zodat wij

En nederig ons hoofd buigen en Hem aanbidden.

Around the world, but particularly in the United States, people seem to value rugged individualism. People who demonstrate this character quality make their own way through life, asking nothing from others and expecting nothing.

I suppose that this idea relates back to the pioneers. These were men and women who trekked across the various new countries looking for a place where they could settle down and call home. There were few general stores and as much as possible they lived as self-sufficiently as they could.

While this may sound like a scenario that demonstrates strength, the truth is somewhat different these days. These days people use technology to deliberately create bubbles of isolation around themselves.

Many older people have found themselves increasingly isolated from friends and family. COVID certainly made this worse, but there were seeds of this seclusion that had been sowed long before COVID was ever heard of.

Isolation is Not a Natural State

Looking back to the Garden of Eden we can see that Adam was created before Eve. While there were lots of animals around, there was no true companionship for Adam. And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him … And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him –Genesis 2:18-20.

And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man –Genesis 2:21-22. Of course, this was the beginning of marriage, but the more important thing to see here is that it is not a normal state for humans to be alone. We desire companionship and not just the companionship of a pet dog or cat.

Isolation can lead to Despair

Perhaps there is no story that demonstrates so clearly the dangers of isolation as the story of Elijah. We know from the biblical book of I Kings, that Elijah was a fiery prophet of God.

He brought word from God to Ahab that there would be no rain and there was terrible drought for the next three and a half years. During that time, Elijah spent time in the wilderness and then with a widow in Zarephath.

The whole time, he was miraculously fed through God’s power, first by ravens and then through God’s provision of flour and oil to a widow, with whom he lived. Through God’s power, he raised the widow’s son to life.

Then came a time when he challenged the prophets of Baal to a match on Mt. Carmel and won a decisive victory for God. Miraculous fire descended from heaven in answer to his prayer. Truly, God was working great things in his life.

Very soon though, Elijah was running for his life into the desert. Jezebel had threatened his life and rather than trusting God, he fled to Mt. Horeb where he heard the voice of God.

When God asked him what he was doing there, Elijah replied, …I have been very jealous for the LORD God of hosts: for the children of Israel have forsaken thy covenant, thrown down thine altars, and slain thy prophets with the sword; and I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away –1 Kings 19:10.

We can see here a big reason for Elijah’s weakness. He felt completely alone. God corrected Elijah’s incorrect assumption when He stated: Yet I have left me seven thousand in Israel, all the knees which have not bowed unto Baal, and every mouth which hath not kissed him –1 Kings 19:18.

The fact that those men and women existed in Israel did Elijah little good since he didn’t spend time with them. Elijah’s isolation led him to weakness and despair.

The story of Paul comes to mind as well. The Apostle Paul was a man who seemed to have nearly limitless amounts of energy and an unquenchable zeal for the things of God, but his last letter to Timothy from prison revealed a man who felt very alone. Do thy diligence to come shortly unto me: For Demas hath forsaken me, having loved this present world, and is departed unto Thessalonica; Crescens to Galatia, Titus unto Dalmatia. Only Luke is with me. Take Mark, and bring him with thee… –2 Timothy 4:9-11.

The Apostle was not abandoned. Other than Demas, they had not fled because they were afraid or ashamed of his bonds. He had sent many of his friends away to strengthen the church in various parts of the Roman Empire. Yet, Paul was still feeling isolated and needed the good Christian brothers, Timothy and Mark, to come and encourage him as he faced a martyr’s death.

Isolation is Physically Harmful

Studies have showed that isolation is linked to higher rates of high blood pressure, heart disease, anxiety, and depression. Older people who are isolated often show signs of mental decline and can experience worsening dementia.

Many times, as people age, they experience the deaths of loved ones. The loss of a spouse can lead older people to withdraw from others and to experience loneliness and isolation. This in turn often leads to rapid progression of the aging process.

Science does not fully understand it, but loneliness leads to increased inflammation and poorer immune function. This in turn can lead to lonely people getting worse infections and struggling to recover after such an infection.

While we think of these problems as those that primarily affect elderly people, they can affect younger people as well. In younger people, often loneliness doesn’t lead to memory issues, but it certainly can lead to things like depression, and it can make chronic inflammatory diseases much worse.

The Opposite of Isolation

If asked what the opposite of isolation is most people would probably answer “Companionship” or maybe even “Friendship”. There is another word which has a Christian connotation that is even better. That word is fellowship.

The Greek word translated fellowship in the New Testament is “Koinonia” and in the Bible it speaks of relationships that are founded on a shared love for God and for the church—a unity of belief and desire. Christian fellowship includes concepts like praying together, encouraging one another, and even suffering together.

I am afraid that many today find themselves in one of two dangerous situations. First, they may not be a member of any church congregation. While this may be unavoidable in certain mission outreach situations, it is not ideal, and most certainly it should not be a normal situation. At the very least it can create a sense of isolation, and at the worst it hinders many of the “one-anothering” Bible passages from being followed. We need fellowship, both to encourage us and to keep us accountable.

The second dangerous situation is that many believers, while members of a church, isolate themselves within that church. If you are a member of a large church congregation, it is easy to blend in and not develop relationships with others. This is just as harmful as not being a member of a church body. Too many people feel lonely, even when there are lots of people around.

Scripture makes it clear that we need a church body. Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together, as the manner of some is; but exhorting one another: and so much the more, as ye see the day approaching –Hebrews 10:25.

There are many people who have lives that are full of friends and acquaintances, but if they do not have a place where they receive fellowship, they are missing out.

When I see people in my office who are struggling with depression there are two things I always tell them to do for themselves.

First is to start exercising. There have been several studies that compared exercise to antidepressants and found that it had similar effectiveness to many of the commonly prescribed antidepressant medications. This doesn’t have to be really vigorous exercise, but it does need to be aerobic (enough to raise the heart rate) and consistent.

The second is to become active in a church congregation; it is not enough to just attend church. Having brothers and sisters to pray for someone who is struggling, to listen to the discouraging situations, and to encourage that person to a more vibrant walk with God is really helpful.

Unfortunately, when someone is struggling with depression, the last thing they seem to want to do is make the effort to be around other people, which contrary to their feelings, is counterproductive to changing the problem.

As we consider this, it should move us to reach out to those who we know are struggling with isolation.

When someone loses a spouse, they often have a lot of encouragement for the first several weeks, but we need to make certain that they continue to have an active presence in their lives in the months that follow.

For every man shall bear his own burden –Galatians 6:5, should not give us excuse to not obey God’s command to Bear ye one another's burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ –Galatians 6:2. The family of God is given no time limit on bearing burdens. There is only a mandate that as we see our brother or sister struggling, we are to help them, as we are able.

The blessing is that someday, when we are struggling, we will have men and women of faith around us to encourage us and to pray for us. We cannot carry these burdens alone. Together, we will reach the Celestial City.

Isolation comes for many reasons. Sometimes it seems to be a chosen way of life, as is the natural tendency of introverted people. Sometimes it is foisted upon a person due to deaths of loved ones or other significant losses. Either way, it is not a healthy place to live.

As we find ourselves in these situations, we need to reach out for fellowship. The family of God is there for us if we only reach out.

As we see others who are struggling, we need to extend to them the right arm of fellowship. As we do so, we may, through our small efforts, help someone emotionally, physically, and spiritually, simply by being a friend in a time of isolation.

Partout dans le monde, mais particulièrement aux États-Unis, les gens semblent valoriser l’individualisme robuste. Les personnes qui manifestent cette qualité de caractère se débrouillent seules dans la vie, ne demandant rien aux autres et n’attendant rien d’eux.

Je suppose que cette idée remonte aux pionniers. C’étaient des hommes et des femmes qui traversaient divers pays nouveaux à la recherche d’un endroit où s’établir et appeler « chez eux ». Il y avait peu d’épiceries générales et, autant que possible, ils vivaient aussi autonome que possible.

Si cela peut sembler décrire une situation qui témoigne de force, la vérité est quelque peu différente de nos jours. Aujourd’hui, les gens utilisent la technologie pour créer délibérément des bulles d’isolement autour d’eux.

Beaucoup de personnes âgées se sont retrouvées de plus en plus isolées de leurs amis et de leur famille. Le COVID a certainement aggravé la situation, mais des graines de ce repli avaient été semées bien avant qu’on n’entende parler du COVID.

L’isolement n’est pas un état naturel

En regardant en arrière jusqu’au Jardin d’Éden, nous voyons qu’Adam fut créé avant Ève. Bien qu’il y eût beaucoup d’animaux, il n’y avait pas de véritable compagnie pour Adam. Et l’Éternel Dieu dit: Il n'est pas bon que l'homme soit seul; je lui ferai une aide semblable à lui… Et Adam donna des noms à tout le bétail, et aux oiseaux du ciel, et à toutes les bêtes des champs; mais pour Adam il ne se trouva point d'aide semblable à lui –Genèse 2:18-20.

Et l'Éternel Dieu fit tomber un profond sommeil sur l'homme, qui s'endormit; il prit une de ses côtes, et referma la chair à sa place. Et la côte qu'il avait prise à l'homme, l'Éternel Dieu en fit une femme, et l'amena à l'homme –Genèse 2:21-22. Bien sûr, ce fut le commencement du mariage, mais l’essentiel ici est que l’état d’être seul n’est pas normal pour les humains. Nous désirons la compagnie et pas seulement la compagnie d’un chien ou d’un chat de compagnie.

L’isolement peut conduire au désespoir

Peut-être n’y a‑t‑il pas d’histoire qui illustre aussi clairement les dangers de l’isolement que l’histoire d’Élie. Nous savons, d’après le livre biblique des Rois, qu’Élie était un prophète ardent de Dieu.

Il annonça de la part de Dieu à Achab qu’il n’y aurait pas de pluie et il y eut une terrible sécheresse pendant les trois ans et demi suivants. Pendant ce temps, Élie passa du temps dans le désert puis chez une veuve à Sarepta.

Tout le temps, il fut miraculeusement nourri par la puissance de Dieu, d’abord par des corbeaux puis par la provision divine de farine et d’huile d’une veuve chez qui il vivait. Par la puissance de Dieu, il ramena le fils de la veuve à la vie.

Puis vint un moment où il défia les prophètes de Baal pour un duel sur le mont Carmel et remporta une victoire décisive pour Dieu. Du feu miraculeux descendit du ciel en réponse à sa prière. Vraiment, Dieu accomplissait de grandes choses dans sa vie.

Toutefois, très vite, Élie prit la fuite dans le désert pour sauver sa vie. Jézabel avait menacé sa vie et plutôt que de faire confiance à Dieu, il s’enfuit au mont Horeb où il entendit la voix de Dieu.

Lorsque Dieu lui demanda ce qu’il faisait là, Élie répondit: …J'ai été tout à fait jaloux pour l'Éternel, le Dieu des armées; car les enfants d'Israël ont abandonné ton alliance, ils ont renversé tes autels, et tes prophètes ils ont mis à mort par l'épée; et moi, je suis resté seul, et ils cherchent mon âme pour la mettre à mort –1 Rois 19:10.

Nous pouvons voir ici une grande raison de la faiblesse d’Élie. Il se sentait complètement seul. Dieu corrigea l’hypothèse erronée d’Élie en déclarant : Cependant, j'ai laissé en Israël sept mille hommes, tous les genoux qui ne se sont pas inclinés devant Baal, et toute bouche qui ne l'a pas baisé –1 Rois 19:18.

Le fait que ces hommes et ces femmes existaient en Israël ne fut d’aucune utilité pour Élie puisqu’il ne passait pas de temps avec eux. L’isolement d’Élie le mena à la faiblesse et au désespoir.

L’histoire de Paul me vient aussi à l’esprit. L’apôtre Paul semblait être un homme ayant presque des quantités illimitées d’énergie et un zèle inextinguible pour les choses de Dieu, mais sa dernière lettre à Timothée depuis la prison révèle un homme qui se sentait très seul. Efforce-toi d'arriver bientôt chez moi: Car Démas m'a abandonné, l'ayant aimé du présent siècle, et il est allé à Thessalonique; Crescens à la Galatie, Tite à la Dalmatie. Seul Luc est avec moi. Prends Marc, et apporte-le toi-même… –2 Timothée 4:9-11.

L’apôtre n’avait pas été abandonné. À l’exception de Démas, ils n’étaient pas partis par peur ou honte de ses chaînes. Il avait envoyé beaucoup de ses amis fortifier l’Église dans diverses parties de l’Empire romain. Pourtant, Paul se sentait isolé et avait besoin que les bons frères chrétiens, Timothée et Marc, viennent l’encourager alors qu’il faisait face à une mort de martyr.

L’isolement est nuisible physiquement

Des études ont montré que l’isolement est lié à des taux plus élevés d’hypertension, de maladies cardiaques, d’anxiété et de dépression. Les personnes âgées isolées montrent souvent des signes de déclin mental et peuvent voir leur démence s’aggraver.

Souvent, en vieillissant, les gens vivent la mort de proches. La perte d’un conjoint peut conduire les personnes âgées à se retirer des autres et à éprouver la solitude et l’isolement. Cela conduit souvent à une progression rapide du processus de vieillissement.

La science ne comprend pas entièrement le phénomène, mais la solitude entraîne une augmentation de l’inflammation et une diminution de l’efficacité du système immunitaire. Cela peut à son tour faire en sorte que les personnes vivant dans la solitude contractent de pires infections et peinent à se rétablir après une telle infection.

Bien que nous pensions que ces problèmes touchent principalement les personnes âgées, ils peuvent également affecter les plus jeunes. Chez les jeunes, la solitude ne conduit pas souvent à des problèmes de mémoire, mais elle peut certainement entraîner des choses comme la dépression, et elle peut aggravir considérablement les maladies inflammatoires chroniques.

Le contraire de l’isolement

Si on demande quel est le contraire de l’isolement, la plupart répondraient probablement « la compagnie » ou peut‑être « l’amitié ». Il existe un autre mot, de connotation chrétienne, qui est encore mieux. Ce mot est la communion.

Le mot grec traduit par communion dans le Nouveau Testament est « koinonia » et dans la Bible il parle de relations fondées sur un amour partagé pour Dieu et pour l’Église — une unité de croyance et de désir. La communion chrétienne inclut des concepts tels que prier ensemble, s’encourager mutuellement, et même souffrir ensemble.

Je crains que beaucoup aujourd’hui se trouvent dans l’une des deux situations dangereuses suivantes. Premièrement, ils peuvent ne pas être membres d’aucune congrégation ecclésiale. Bien que cela puisse être inévitable dans certaines situations de mission, ce n’est pas l’idéal, et cela ne devrait certainement pas être une situation normale. Au minimum, cela peut créer un sentiment d’isolement, et au pire cela empêche l’observation de nombreux passages bibliques qui commandent le « les-uns-les-autres ». Nous avons besoin de communion, à la fois pour nous encourager et pour nous garder responsables.

La deuxième situation dangereuse est que beaucoup de croyants, bien que membres d’une Église, s’isolent au sein même de cette Église. Si vous êtes membre d’une grande congrégation, il est facile de se fondre dans la masse et de ne pas développer de relations avec les autres. C’est tout aussi nuisible que de ne pas être membre d’un corps ecclésial. Trop de gens se sentent seuls, même lorsqu’il y a beaucoup de monde autour d’eux.

Les Écritures affirment clairement que nous avons besoin d’un corps ecclésial. N'abandonnant pas notre assemblée, comme quelques-uns en ont l'habitude, mais nous exhortant réciproquement, et cela d'autant plus que vous voyez s'approcher le jour –Hébreux 10:25.

Il y a beaucoup de personnes dont la vie est pleine d’amis et de connaissances, mais si elles n’ont pas un lieu où elles reçoivent la communion, elles passent à côté de quelque chose.

Quand je vois des personnes dans mon cabinet qui luttent contre la dépression, il y a deux choses que je leur dis toujours de faire pour elles‑mêmes.

La première est de commencer à faire de l’exercice. Plusieurs études ont comparé l’exercice aux antidépresseurs et ont trouvé qu’il avait une efficacité similaire à celle de nombreux médicaments antidépresseurs couramment prescrits. Il ne s’agit pas nécessairement d’un exercice très intense, mais il doit être aérobie (suffisant pour élever le rythme cardiaque) et régulier.

La seconde est de devenir actif au sein d’une congrégation; il ne suffit pas d’assister à l’église. Avoir des frères et sœurs pour prier pour une personne en difficulté, écouter des situations décourageantes et encourager cette personne à avoir une marche plus vivante avec Dieu est d’un grand secours.

Malheureusement, quand quelqu’un souffre de dépression, la dernière chose qu’il semble vouloir faire est de faire l’effort d’être parmi d’autres personnes, ce qui, contrairement à ce qu’il ressent, est contre‑productif pour résoudre le problème.

À la réflexion, cela devrait nous pousser à tendre la main à ceux que nous savons être aux prises avec l’isolement.

Lorsqu’une personne perd son conjoint, elle reçoit souvent beaucoup d’encouragements pendant les premières semaines, mais nous devons veiller à ce qu’elle continue d’avoir une présence active dans sa vie dans les mois qui suivent.

Car chacun portera sa propre charge –Galates 6:5, ne devrait pas nous donner d’excuse pour ne pas obéir au commandement de Dieu de Porter les fardeaux les uns des autres, et vous accomplirez ainsi la loi de Christ –Galates 6:2. La famille de Dieu n’a pas de limite de temps pour porter les fardeaux. Il n’y a qu’un mandat : lorsque nous voyons notre frère ou notre sœur en difficulté, nous devons l’aider, autant que nous le pouvons.

La bénédiction est que, un jour, quand nous serons en difficulté, il y aura des hommes et des femmes de foi autour de nous pour nous encourager et prier pour nous. Nous ne pouvons pas porter ces fardeaux seuls. Ensemble, nous atteindrons la Cité céleste.

L’isolement survient pour de nombreuses raisons. Parfois, il semble être un mode de vie choisi, comme c’est la tendance naturelle des personnes introverties. Parfois, il est imposé à une personne en raison de la mort de proches ou d’autres pertes significatives. Quoi qu’il en soit, ce n’est pas un lieu sain où vivre.

Lorsque nous nous trouvons dans de telles situations, nous devons chercher la communion. La famille de Dieu est là pour nous si nous tendons simplement la main.

Lorsque nous voyons d’autres personnes en difficulté, nous devons leur tendre le bras droit de la communion. Ce faisant, par nos petits efforts, nous pourrons aider quelqu’un émotionnellement, physiquement et spirituellement, simplement en étant un ami en temps d’isolement.

When you, my friend, are standing on this earth
And gazing up into the firmament
Where stretches all of space, what do you see?
A great black blanket stretched o’er all the sky
With many a mystery light somewhere up there?
Or can you see the distances so great
Which stretch the mind almost to breaking point
And make you feel the size you really are?
In the still silence of the spacious sky,
The far-off planets seem almost in reach
Compared to the great distance to the stars.
The crescent moon is closer yet to you,
And yet it took man three whole days to reach
That tiny sphere so very close at hand.
But what you see while gazing up to heights
Which you cannot begin to comprehend
Is but a streak of all the vast expanse
Beyond the knowledge of this human race.
And so, my friend, I hope that you will feel
That greatness, vastness, emptiness of space
Which our Creator made for us so we
Can feel His greatness and His tender love
And humbly bow our heads and worship Him.

–by Daniel Kaufman

När du, min vän, står på denna jord
Och ser upp mot det fasta valvet där
Som rymmer allting, vad är det du ser?
En stor svart filt utspänd över skyn
Med många ljus som något mysterium där?
Eller ser du avstånden så stora
Som tänjs till bristningsgränsens rand
Och får dig att känna hur liten du är?
I den stilla tystnad i det vida sky
Verkar de avlägsna planeterna nästan nåbara
Jämfört med de stora avstånd till stjärnorna.
Den slanka månskäran är ännu närmare dig,
Och ändå tog det människan tre hela dagar
Att nå den lilla klotet så nära till hands.
Men vad du ser när du blickar upp mot höjder
Som du inte börjar kunna begripa
Är bara en remsa av den enorma rymd
Bortom denna människoras kännedom.
Så, min vän, jag hoppas att du ska känna
Den storhet, vidhet, tomhet i rymden
Som vår Skapare gjorde för oss så att vi
Kan känna Hans storhet och Hans ömma kärlek
Och ödmjukt böja våra huvuden och tillbe Honom.

–av Daniel Kaufman

There is coming a day when all will be well.
The things that are bad will all be in hell.
But we must not forget that day has not come.
We are in a battle; we must still overcome.
The enemy rages, his time here is short.
He spreads all his lies, the truth to distort.
Sin in our lives, it is his great goal.
For he knows very well it will cost us our soul.
It need not be big; a small sin will do.
He’ll trick and deceive, each soul to pursue.
The darts of the wicked come from all sides.
When faced with God’s power, that devil—he hides!
When God is with us, he cannot advance!
When God is with us, sin has no chance!
For the eyes of the Lord seek to and fro,
To find one perfect, His power He’ll show!
Let’s be done with the lesser and look far beyond.
Let’s take hold of God’s power! It’s time to respond!
